```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

Most keys already exist: as text in a flora, a revision or a field guide. This
vignette takes one from the printed page to a phone in five steps: read the
text, check it, cut it down to the place you work in, see how quickly it
reaches a result, and export it as a page that opens without signal.

The steps that ask a web service (GBIF) are shown with the output of a run on
19 November 2026 and are not run when the vignette is built. Everything else
runs as written.

```{r}
library(dimoose)
```

## 1. Read the text

The example is a short key to the broadleaf trees of a river bottom, written
for dimoose in the layout of a regional flora: numbered couplets with `a` and
`b` leads, dot leaders, wrapped lines, authorities, common names and page
references.

```{r}
file <- system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "trees-bracketed.txt", package = "dimoose")
writeLines(readLines(file)[1:11])
```

`keyFromText()` takes a file, one string or a vector of lines:

```{r}
trees <- keyFromText(file)
trees
trees$leads[1:6, c("Statement", "Choice", "Character", "Next", "Taxon", "CommonName")]
```

Each lead's destination is a couplet number or a taxon. The authority, the
common name and the page are split off into columns of their own, so `Taxon`
holds the bare name. It also reads leads marked `1.`/`1'.`, `A.`/`AA.`, a
number and a dash, back-references such as `3(1).`, and indented keys. Indented
keys whose leads have no number or letter at all are not handled.

## 2. Check it

`keyFromText()` checks what it built and keeps a report with the key. Here
the only entry is a note: a word hyphenated at a line end was joined.

```{r}
trees$validate()          # no structural problems
attr(trees, "problems")
```

Scanned text is rougher. `parseTextKey()` gives the lead table and the report
without building the key, which is the place to start with a scan. This one
has a `l` where a `1` should be and a lead that lost its dot leaders:

```{r}
scan <- system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "meadow-ocr.txt", package = "dimoose")
parseTextKey(scan)
```

Repairs are reported, never silent, and `strict = TRUE` stops instead of
repairing. A lead with no destination, a couplet with one lead or a missing
couplet is a problem, reported with its line; no lead is dropped. These
checks were written against keys made for the purpose; expect to correct a
few lines by hand on a real scan.

A printed key's names may be out of date. `checkNames()` looks them up in the
GBIF backbone taxonomy:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
checkNames(trees, kingdom = "Plantae")[, c("Taxon", "status", "accepted")]
#>                                    Taxon  status               accepted
#> 1                           Acer glabrum      ok           Acer glabrum
#> 2                           Acer negundo      ok           Acer negundo
#> 3                 Fraxinus pennsylvanica      ok Fraxinus pennsylvanica
#> 4                                  Salix      ok                  Salix
#> 5                      Betula papyrifera      ok      Betula papyrifera
#> 6                    Betula occidentalis      ok    Betula occidentalis
#> 7                    Populus tremuloides      ok    Populus tremuloides
#> 8                   Populus angustifolia      ok   Populus angustifolia
#> 9 Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa synonym    Populus trichocarpa
```

## 3. Cut it down to a place

A regional flora covers more than any one county. `regionalKey()` asks GBIF
which of the key's taxa have been recorded in a place, drops the others, and
closes up the couplets that no longer split anything. Here the place is
Flathead County, Montana, by its GADM id, and a taxon needs five records to
stay:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
local <- regionalKey(trees, "USA.27.15_1", kingdom = "Plantae", minRecords = 5, renumber = TRUE)
#> Kept 8 of 9 taxa recorded in GADM region USA.27.15_1 (GBIF)
attr(local, "records")[, c("Taxon", "records", "kept")]
#>                                    Taxon records  kept
#> 1                           Acer glabrum     272  TRUE
#> 2                           Acer negundo      11  TRUE
#> 3                 Fraxinus pennsylvanica       1 FALSE
#> 4                                  Salix     348  TRUE
#> 5                      Betula papyrifera      70  TRUE
#> 6                    Betula occidentalis      13  TRUE
#> 7                    Populus tremuloides      93  TRUE
#> 8                   Populus angustifolia       7  TRUE
#> 9 Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa      56  TRUE
```

The table is the audit trail: every taxon, the number of records and whether
it was kept. A place can also be a name (`"Flathead County, Montana"`), a
two-letter country code or a polygon, and `source = "inat"` counts
iNaturalist research-grade observations instead. With the default
`minRecords = 1` all nine taxa of this key stay. Record counts say where
people have looked as much as what grows there, so read the table before
trusting the cut.

`pruneKey()` makes the same cut from a list of names, with no web service.
So that the rest of this vignette runs offline, it is used here to drop the
one taxon GBIF dropped above:

```{r}
local <- pruneKey(trees, drop = "Fraxinus pennsylvanica", renumber = TRUE)
local
local$validate()
local$leads[1:4, c("Statement", "Character", "Next", "Taxon", "Note")]
```

Couplet 3 of the original told box elder from green ash. With green ash
gone it no longer splits anything, so it was removed and its lead now ends at
box elder directly. What it said about box elder is kept in the `Note`
column, as a character to confirm the result with. `mergeKeys()` goes the
other way and grafts a second key onto a result, for example a key to the
willows onto *Salix*.

## 4. How quickly does it reach a result?

```{r}
summary(local)[c("couplets", "taxa", "depth", "meanTaxonSteps", "bound", "efficiency")]
```

`meanTaxonSteps` is the number of couplets a reader answers, on average over
the eight taxa. `bound` is what the best possible key to the same taxa would
need: eight equally common taxa cannot be told apart in fewer than three
two-way steps. `efficiency` is the bound over the steps taken.

The taxa are not equally likely, though. Weighted by the record counts above
(which `occurrenceWeights(local, region = "USA.27.15_1", kingdom = "Plantae")`
fetches in one call), the key does better than its plain average, because
the two commonest taxa key out in two steps:

```{r}
w <- c("Acer glabrum" = 272, "Acer negundo" = 11, "Salix" = 348, "Betula papyrifera" = 70,
       "Betula occidentalis" = 13, "Populus tremuloides" = 93, "Populus angustifolia" = 7,
       "Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa" = 56)
summary(local, weights = w)[c("meanTaxonSteps", "expectedSteps", "bound", "efficiency")]
q <- keyQuality(local, weights = w)$taxa
q[order(-q$weight), c("Taxon", "steps", "weight")]
```

Real keys rarely reach an efficiency of 1, because the characters that would
split the taxa evenly may not exist. Use it to compare keys to the same
taxa, not as a mark out of one.

## 5. Take it into the field

```{r}
site <- file.path(tempdir(), "site")
dir.create(site, showWarnings = FALSE)
page <- exportWizard(local, file.path(site, "flathead-trees.html"), offline = TRUE)
list.files(site)
```

`flathead-trees.html` is the whole key in one file: it asks one couplet at a
time, has an "I'm not sure" choice that follows both leads, a map of the key,
and Back. `offline = TRUE` adds a web app manifest, a service worker and two
icons. Put all five files in one folder of an `https` website, open the page
once on the phone while it has a connection, and add it to the home screen;
after that it opens without signal. A page opened straight from disk works
too, but is not installed. The offline part has been tested with a simulated
browser and not yet on a phone, so try it before you rely on it.

To correct a lead or add photos, write the key out as the spreadsheet
`keyFromSpreadsheet()` reads, edit it, and read it back (see
`vignette("montana-hardwoods")`):

```{r}
csv <- keyToSpreadsheet(local, file.path(site, "flathead-trees.csv"))
back <- keyFromSpreadsheet(csv, desc = "Trees of Flathead County")
back
```

The spreadsheet keeps the leads and their photos; the title and the extra
columns (`Note`, `Authority`, `CommonName`, `Page`) are not written.
